content_voiceover: This slide shows the normal control for platelet glycoprotein flow cytometry, the test used to diagnose Glanzmann thrombasthenia. On flow cytometry, CD41 marks glycoprotein IIb and CD61 marks glycoprotein IIIa, and in a healthy subject both are essentially one hundred percent positive, and they co-express together as the intact GPIIb-IIIa complex, the fibrinogen receptor on platelets. The bottom panels show PAC-1 binding, an antibody that only binds the activated conformation of GPIIb-IIIa. At baseline, PAC-1 positivity is low, around six percent, but after stimulating with five micromolar ADP, PAC-1 binding jumps to about ninety-two percent, confirming normal agonist-induced activation of the integrin. Keep this normal pattern in mind as your reference point, because the next slide will show a patient with Glanzmann thrombasthenia where GPIIb-IIIa expression and activation are both markedly reduced. For boards, remember Glanzmann thrombasthenia is an autosomal recessive disorder of GPIIb-IIIa, ITGA2B or ITGB3 mutations, causing failure of platelet aggregation despite a normal platelet count.
keypoints: PAC-1 detects the activated GPIIb/IIIa conformation
Normal reference for Glanzmann thrombasthenia workup
keypoint_voiceover: In the normal control, CD41 and CD61, marking GPIIb and GPIIIa, are both fully expressed at one hundred percent, and they pair together as the intact fibrinogen receptor. PAC-1 antibody detects the activated form of this receptor, and stimulation with five micromolar ADP boosts PAC-1 binding from a baseline of six percent up to ninety-two percent. This is the healthy baseline you compare against when working up suspected Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
